about: The words of the chain 'barrow' (Data/encounters/chain_barrow_793.json; Design/content/chains/barrow.md). Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite. Keys: chain_barrow.sNN.<what>; an option's outcome is chain_barrow.sNN.out_<option> (and _success, _failure after a chance); art.<card id> says what the card's picture shows. Nothing is quoted from any translation: Bede, Felix and the dragon song are retold in the speakers' own words.

entries.text: The fowler's word

A fowler sells duck and teal from a pole on the strand at Gipeswic. He has come down from the Deben, the next river up the coast, and he has something on his mind besides birds. He says it to you because you are a stranger and will be gone on the ebb.
Duck, teal, a heron if your lord is proud. Taken this morning on the Deben, the next river north. The river is full of them since the gale.
You will have seen the hoe from the water, if you have been up there. A long hill over the east bank with humps along its back, like loaves on a board. Those are the old kings. Nobody ploughs there.
The reeve hangs thieves up there now, on one of the smaller humps. He says it saves a cart. They go into the ground beside it, face down, next to the kings. I do not know what the kings think.

The gale put a thorn tree down on the hump at the river end and took the side out with it. I went up for the wood. There is something yellow in the sand under the roots. I looked at it for a while. Then I looked at the gallows, and I came down.
We have a king of our own again, a young one. He strikes pennies with a she-wolf on them. The Mercians let him, so far.
We had a king of our own until Offa had his head off. It is a Mercian's reeve now. He hangs more.
Buy a brace of duck (4 d) and ask him the way in over the Deben bar

He draws the bar in the sand with a duck's foot. Keep the dead oak over the ferry landing, go in on the last quarter of the flood, and trust nothing you saw last year: the shingle moves every winter. The ducks are fat. The men eat them before the boat is afloat.
Ask him whose dead they are

Wuffa's kin, he says. Kings here before the cross came, and one or two after it who were not sure which way to face. His grandmother knew their names in order. He knows the humps. Your lookout, who was a monk's boy once, has stopped pretending not to listen.
Tell him dead kings are no cargo of yours
He shrugs, and sells you nothing. But the men heard every word. On the way back to the boat the Northman asks, of nobody, which way the Deben lies, and the steersman tells him before he has thought.

The strand at Gipeswic on a bright windy morning: a lean fowler with a pole of dead duck over his shoulder points north along the coast; a small clinker boat on the mud behind him, four men turning to listen.
The hoe

The Deben opens two hours up the coast. The flood is making, and the men are looking at you and not at the sail. You go in over the bar and up between the mud banks until the hoe stands over the east shore: eighteen or twenty mounds along the hill's back, and a gallows on one. At the river end a thorn tree lies on its side with its roots in the air. Under the roots the mound is open, like a loaf with the end cut off.
There. Under the root. That is not a stone.

It is a strap mount as long as a thumb. Gold, set with red stones cut in steps, each stone in its own small cell. The sand has run out from around it. Further in there is the green rim of a bronze bowl, and something that was wood.
That is a grave. A man was laid here, with what his people gave him. They gave it to him. They did not give it to us.
A heathen, and gone where heathens go. The gold did him no good. I do not say it would do us any.
The fowler's dead oak was where he said. The reeve's herd is on the far side of the hill, and there is nobody on the river.
Take the gold mount that shows, and nothing more
It comes away from the sand as if it had been waiting. It is heavier than it looks. You wrap it in a rag and put it in the chest under the pennies. Nobody speaks until the boat is over the bar.
Dig with the bailer and your hands for one tide

The sand is soft and runs. In an hour you have the gold mount, a silver buckle black as a coal, and the rim of the bronze bowl with burnt bone in it. Then roof timbers, soft as cheese, and the tide turning. You take the gold and the buckle and leave the bone.

The sand is soft and runs, and it goes on running after you want it to stop. Half the side comes down. When you stand up with the gold mount in your hand there is a herdsman on the far bank, leaning on his staff, in no hurry. He has had a long look at the boat.
Touch nothing. Pull turf down over the break

The Northman cuts turf with his knife and the Saxon carries it. It takes most of the ebb. When it is done the gold is under a hand's depth of grass, and the mound looks only as if a tree had fallen on it. The lookout says a psalm. Nobody tells him not to.

A long bare hill over a tidal river at low grey noon: a row of grass mounds, a gallows on one; in front a fallen thorn tree with its roots in the air over a break of yellow sand; four men standing well back from one small red and gold thing.
Four men and a dead one
That night, at anchor behind the shingle, nobody sleeps. The men have been turning the hoe over since the bar, each by himself. Now they do it aloud.

I will say it plainly. I do not want that thing in the boat unblessed. Take it to the bishop at Dommoc. Gold that goes through a priest's hands comes out a cup for the altar. That is the only clean road I know for it.
We did right. Others will come, and they will not. Tell the bishop at Dommoc. Let him put a cross on that hill and be done with it.

At Ögvaldsnes they laid a king in his ship and heaped a hill over him. My father carried turf to it. So I know a little about hills. I do not like to say this at night. A man who breaks such a hill has the one inside it walking behind him. I have never heard that such a one gets tired.
Put it back and close the hill. That is my advice. It is all the advice I have, and it is cheap.

My father lies under a hill like that, on the Weser. The king's law says I may not, when my day comes. I am to lie in the church's yard among strangers. So do not ask me whose that gold is. I know whose.

The holy Guthlac lived in a hill like it, in the fens. Greedy men had dug it open before he came, looking for treasure. He found devils in it and no gold. Felix wrote that for a king of this very country. The brothers read it to us at Gyrwe.
And there is a song. A dragon lay on a hoard three hundred winters, and a man took one cup from it. One cup. A whole people burned for that.
Give the steersman your word: the bishop will hear of it
The steersman nods once and is asleep at once, like a man who has put down a load. The Northman looks at the water. A cup for the altar, he says. So the bishop is a mound-breaker with clean hands.
Give the Northman your word: the hill is left to its dead

The Northman says nothing for once, which from him is thanks. The Saxon grips your arm above the elbow and lets go. The steersman says a word given to the dead about heathen gold is a strange thing to take to confession, and that he will carry it there for you if you like.
Hear them all out, and promise nothing

They talk until the tide turns. Nobody is persuaded. To end it the lookout says the dragon song, as much as he has of it, and it is long, and the men are quiet for it. You have it by heart yourself by the time the anchor comes up.

The boat at anchor at night behind a shingle bank, a horn lantern on the thwart: a grey steersman with a wooden cross at his neck speaking, a dark-bearded Northman looking away at the black water, a big Saxon with his arms folded, a thin young Englishman counting on his fingers.
The third day
The Saxon cannot hold his oar. He is hot, then cold, then hot, and his teeth knock together so that the men hear it from the bow. Nobody says the word mound. Everybody is thinking it.

I will say it, since nobody else will. He is not sick. He is followed. Give the sea something for the one in the hill. A little silver, cut, over the lee side. It need not be much. The dead take payment like anybody else.
We took nothing, so it is not that. I keep telling myself so. Still. A little silver over the lee side never made a man worse.
No silver to devils. We fast a day, we say what prayers we have, and I sign him with the cross. And the lid of that chest as well.

He slept two nights with the marsh fog on him. The brothers at Gyrwe called it the spring sickness and gave warm ale with wormwood. It came every third day, and then it stopped coming. I only say what they did.
I can row.
Cut six pennies and give them to the sea, as the Northman asks

The Northman halves the pennies on the gunwale and drops them over the lee side one at a time, saying something each time that you do not catch. The steersman bails with his back to it. On the third day the Saxon's fever does not come.
Fast a day and let the steersman pray over him

A day on water and prayer. The steersman signs the Saxon's forehead, then the mast, then the lid of the chest. The Saxon lets him, as he once let the Franks. On the third day his fever does not come. The Northman says third days are like that.
Take his oar yourself, and give him warm ale and your dry cloak

You row his watch and your own. Your hands open in two places. The Saxon sweats under your cloak and drinks what he is given, and on the third day his fever does not come. He does not thank you. He scrubs the cloak before he gives it back.

The boat under oars on a flat grey sea: a big man wrapped in a cloak shaking against the mast; an old Northman holding a penny over the gunwale on a knife; the steersman with his hand raised to make a cross.
Old work

A goldsmith has his bench in a lean-to behind the moneyer's house at Dorestad. One of your men has talked over ale, or the man simply has a nose. He asks, without looking up, whether a shipman off the English coast has anything old to show him.

Give it here. I will not run off with it, I have a bad leg. Ah. English work, and old, older than your grandfather. Look at the stones. Cut in steps, every one, with a stamped foil under each to throw the light back. Nobody cuts them so now. The stones stopped coming, and then the hands forgot.

This sat on a king's sword belt, or on the belt of a man a king loved. By weight it is a hundred and sixty pennies: one of gold for twelve of silver. I would melt it by evening. I would be sorry by morning. But I would melt it.

Nothing? Your steersman told the alewife otherwise, or told her you had left it lying. A pity. I had one such piece through my hands as a boy. Red stones cut in steps, foil under them. I melted it. I still think about it.
Do not tell me where. I mean it. If you tell me I must decide whether to tell the count, and I am too old to decide things.
But this much for nothing. Where there is a belt mount there was a belt. Where there was a belt there was a man. And such a man did not go into the earth with one thing.
Sell him the gold mount for melting (160 d)

He weighs it twice, against pennies and then against barleycorns, and pays in good new coin. The bellows are going before you are out of the lean-to. The Northman, who waited outside, asks nothing. He has seen your face.
Ask him about the old gold work, and sell nothing

He talks for an hour. Red stones from beyond the Greeks' sea, split with a hot wire, ground on a wheel no wider than a penny. He has a riddle about what his trade is made of, which an Englishman gave him, and he gives you that too. He takes no pay. He says the talking was pay.
Ask what a whole grave of such work would bring

He puts down his tongs. A sword with gold at the hilt. A purse. Buckles. Cups. If it is a king, a helm. He names a sum, and then names it again more quietly. Come after dark, he says, and by the back, and do not bring the Northman: he frightens my wife. He gives you a riddle a Dane once paid him with, so that you will think of him.

A dark lean-to at Dorestad lit by a small charcoal fire: an old goldsmith with a bad leg holds something small and red-gold close to one eye; fine scales, tongs and a crucible on the bench; a tall Northman waiting in the daylight of the doorway.
The distaff side

An old woman sells wool by the fleece at the edge of the market. She has watched your boat since it came in. When you pass she says, in slow careful Frisian, that she hears you have been on the Deben, and that she had people there once.
My mother's mother was of Wuffa's kin, on the distaff side, which counts for nothing and which I have never forgotten. My name is Leofwaru. I can say the kings back to Wuffa. Nobody asks me to.

The great hill at the river end of the hoe, the long one. They say that is Rædwald, who was washed in Kent and came home and kept two altars in one temple: a big one for Christ and a small one for the old ones. Others say it is his son. The hill does not say.
We have a king of our own again, a young one. Offa of the Mercians watches him as a cat watches a wren.
Offa had our king's head off, and he a guest. Now a Mercian's reeve hangs thieves among my kin and calls the hill the king's. Which king, I ask him.
I have bent my knee to three masters in my time and meant it to none. The reeve hangs thieves among my kin and calls the hill the king's. Which king, I ask him.
Somebody has been at the small hill by the fallen thorn. The reeve knows it. He has put a boy with a horn in the alders, and he is asking after boats.
Tell her what you saw on the hoe, all of it

She listens with her hands flat on the fleeces. When you have done she is quiet a while. So it is open, she says. Well. You told me, which the reeve's men would not have. Whatever you do next, come and tell me that too. I should like one person to.
Ask her to say the kings, and say nothing yourself

Wuffa, Tytila, Rædwald, Eorpwald, and on down through Anna and his holy daughters to Ælfwald, who was the last, and after him strangers. She says them like a woman counting stitches. Your lookout mouths them after her. It costs you nothing, and she is pleased for a week.
Ask her whose the gold in such a hill is now

The king says the king's, she says. The bishop says God's. The reeve says the reeve's, when he thinks nobody hears. I say it is the man's who lies on it, and after him nobody's, like his name. She sells you no wool. She had not meant to.

The edge of an English market under a low autumn sun: a straight-backed old woman in a dark head-cloth behind a heap of fleeces, one hand raised with the fingers spread as if counting; behind her the river and a small boat.
The reeve asks after boats

The reeve of Gipeswic is on the strand himself when you come in, which he is not for most boats. Up the coast, on the hoe, a potter's lad from this town has been hanging for nine days. He was found in the small mound by the fallen thorn, up to his waist in it, with a bronze bowl in his arms.

His name was Dudda and he made bad pots. He dug by daylight, which tells you what kind of thief he was. I hanged him over the place and put him in beside it. He had nothing on him but the bowl. Somebody had been there first.
What lies in the king's earth is King Æthelberht's. I did not make that rule and I do not know who did.
What lies in the king's earth is King Offa's now. All of it, as far as the sea.
What lies in the king's earth is the king's. Ask me next year which king. This year I say Eadwald, and I say it quietly.
What lies in the king's earth is King Coenwulf's.
A herdsman on the Deben saw a small boat under the hoe after the gale. Lapped planks, a tanned sail, four men. He is a herdsman. He remembers things that stand still for a while.
A boat was on the Deben after the gale. Nobody will say whose. Yours lay at my strand that week and went out on the next ebb.
A man who comes and tells me a thing is a finder, and a finder has a share by custom. A man I have to find is the other thing. I have rope.
Tell him all of it, as it happened

He hears it standing. He does not write, because he cannot. He has you say it again before two elders of the town. Keep what you hold until the king's word comes, he says. I know where you sell. He takes half toll of you for two months, his trouble being less.
Say you bought duck from a fowler and sailed for home
He looks at you, and at the boat, and at the men, who look at the gulls. Duck, he says. He has no witness who will swear to a face. He lets the ebb take you.

He lets you finish. Then he has a herdsman's boy brought, who points at your steersman's red cap without being asked. It is forty pennies for wasting the king's reeve's morning, and he says the next sum will not be counted in pennies. There is a watch on the hoe from tonight.
Say it is a matter for the bishop, and that you are on your way to him

He does not like it. A reeve cannot hang what a bishop has his hand on, and both of you know it. Then go to him, he says, and tell him the hill is the king's, cross or no cross. He spits, carefully, not toward you.

The strand at Gipeswic in a cold spring wind: a heavy reeve in a good cloak with a staff, two spearmen behind him; far off up the coast, small against the sky, a hill with a gallows and something hanging from it.
The long hill

The Deben again, on the night flood. From the river you can see what Dudda did before they hanged him: the small mound is half out on the grass. Beside it, at the river end, lies the great one, long and whole, with the turf unbroken from end to end. A boy with a horn is supposed to be in the alders. He is asleep, or he is somewhere else.

Look at the shape of it. No, look properly. Long, and highest in the middle. Earth does not lie like that by itself. There is a ship in that. A whole ship, keel and all, and the man amidships under a roof. I know how it is done.
Then it is the king. The one with two altars.
The small one is spoiled already. What is left in it goes to the next potter. I do not say take it. I say that is how it is.
Turf goes back on quicker than it comes off. I have cut enough of it.
The reeve said a watch. It is one boy. But a horn carries a long way over water at night.
You gave your word about this hill. I forget most things. Not that. I only remind you. I do not hold your arm.
Open the great mound from the top: two nights and the day between

You go in from the top, as down a well, and shore the pit with the bottom boards. Sand, then black wood, then a roof fallen in on what it covered. A helm with a man's face. A sword with gold at the hilt. A buckle as heavy as a quern-rubber. A purse of small gold coins. Silver dishes, crushed, with Greek marks on them. You take what four men can carry down a hill twice. The Northman does not dig. He keeps the watch, and he does not look at what comes up.

A night and a day down the middle of it, and nothing but sand and black wood. In the second dusk the horn sounds from the alders, close. You go down the hill with what you had already lifted from the small mound to pay for the trouble: buckles, a blue glass cup, the gold from a sword. The pit stays open behind you, a spear's length short of whatever is there. The Northman says the dead man's luck held, and sounds glad of it.
Clear what the potter left in the small mound, and go

A blue glass cup, whole, which is a wonder. Two buckles. The gold from a sword hilt, and the red stones out of a pouch lid. A bronze bowl gone green, which you leave to the burnt bone in it. It fills a sack a child could carry. The Northman carries nothing.
Lay back what you took, and turf the break over

It takes the whole ebb. The Saxon cuts and the Northman lays, green side up, tight as a wall. Anything you held goes in first, a hand's depth under. When it is done the Northman pours a horn of ale on it. The steersman, after some thought, says an Our Father, since nobody knows for certain who the man was. Both look satisfied.
Look from the river, and go out on the ebb
You lie under the alders for one tide and look. A hill with a ship in it. Then the ebb takes you out over the bar, and nobody has put a foot on the hoe.

Night on a tidal river under a half moon: a long whale-backed mound black against the sky, a smaller mound beside it torn open and pale; a gallows; the small boat nosed into the reeds, four men looking up the slope.
The last voice

With the land going down astern the steersman ships his oar. He says the thing must be settled before the next harbour, because the men will not sit on it another month. Everybody aboard has a voice. You have the last one.
To the bishop at Dommoc. Say what we saw, give him what we hold, and let him make it clean. A cross on that hill, and no more hanging on it.
Back in the earth, and the hill shut. You all knew I would say it. And if it is too late for that, then nowhere that melts it.
The reeve hangs men over it. Give it to him and you give it to his king. I have seen what kings do with what they are given.
The reeve said a finder has a share. I only say he said it. And a king's leave on a boat is worth more than gold in one.
The goldsmith at Dorestad said to come after dark.
You gave me your word once, behind the shingle.
You gave me your word once. I have not spoken of it since, and you know how I talk.
I have turned it every way I know. With what is under the boards now, it cannot go back. Not past a watch that is awake. I know it. I say it so that nobody need say it to me.
Back into the earth, and word of it to the old kings' kin

You go in once more on a night flood. What is aboard goes back where it lay, and the turf over it. Then there is only an old woman at Gipeswic to tell. The Northman takes the steering oar without being asked and holds it all the way out over the bar, which he has never done.
To the bishop at Dommoc
The steersman lays the course for Dommoc before you have finished the sentence. The Northman says a bishop is a king with a book, and takes his oar.
To the king's reeve at Gipeswic, for the finder's share
The lookout was right about the king's leave, and knows it, and is not happy to be right. The Saxon rows for two days without a word.
To the goldsmith at Dorestad, after dark
Nobody says anything. That is the men's answer. The steersman lays the course for the Rhine mouth. That night the Northman moves his sea chest to the bow, as far from yours as the boat allows.

The boat at sea in clear evening light, the English shore a low line astern: the steersman with his oar shipped, three men turned on the thwarts toward the viewer, waiting; a sea chest between them with its lid shut.
Green side up

Leofwaru is at the edge of the market with her fleeces, and the fowler is with her. She has heard already: a hill does not get turfed on the Deben without the fowlers knowing by the next tide. She has put on a ring you have not seen before.
Sæwine walked the hoe on Sunday. He says the break is shut, green side up, laid by somebody who has laid turf before. He says he would not find it now if he did not know.

I have nothing a king would call wealth. I have wool rents from three farms, a toft by the quay that my husband left, and this ring, which was my mother's mother's and came out of no hill. Choose. Do not be polite about it.
And I will show you the bar. All of it: the winter channel, the summer one, and where it goes after a north-easter. I have shown nobody. My sons do not want it.
The Mercian will dig it himself one day, or his son will. But not this year, and not because of a Frisian. That is something to have been.
This year a boat of Dorestad lay under the hoe on the Deben. The men took nothing away, and the mound was closed.
Take the toft by the quay

The toft is forty feet of the Orwell's bank, with a hazel fence and a well lined with an old wine cask. She has two elders witness it and puts a turf from it in your hand. With it come six hundred pennies in three kings' coin, the wool rents of two years. The fowler takes you over the Deben bar on the next flood and makes you say it back to him.
Take the ring

She works it off over the knuckle with spit. Gold, plain, with a wolf's head where the ends meet. For your son, she says, or whoever has the boat after you. Tell him whose it was, and that it was given. With it come nine hundred pennies in three kings' coin. The fowler takes you over the Deben bar on the next flood and makes you say it back to him.

The hoe on a clear morning seen from the river: every mound whole and green, the fallen thorn gone for firewood; on the bank an old woman and a fowler; she is holding out one hand with a gold ring on the palm.
A cup for the altar

The bishop of the East Angles receives you in the porch of his church at Dommoc, with the sea loud behind it. He is an old man with ink on his thumb. He has heard the steersman first, which was the steersman's idea. Now he hears you.

When the blessed Gregory sent Mellitus to the English he told him: do not pull down their temples. Cast out the idols, sprinkle the walls, set up altars. A people goes on coming to the place it knows. I have always thought it the wisest letter a pope ever wrote.

So. Gold out of a heathen hill is still gold. God made it before any heathen laid a hand on it. Gold from that hill will be a cup for this altar and a cover for the gospels, and of more use there than it was to him.

And if it is Rædwald: he was baptised, in Kent. A poor sort of Christian, with his two altars. So are most men. I can say a Mass for a poor sort of Christian. I will not say whose it is, and nobody will ask me.
I will have a cross of oak set on the hoe, at the river end. The reeve can find another hill for his rope.
A helm with a man's face. A king's whole gear. I had thought such things were only in the songs my clerks are not supposed to know.
This year word of the old kings' mounds on the Deben was brought to the bishop at Dommoc, and a cross was set up there.
Take the church's freight, and the bishop's hand over the boat

His men will dig the small hill themselves, with a priest standing by, and what they find comes here. To you: six hundred and fifty pennies, paid before the voyage, for the church's wine and wax for a year, and an order for four casks more. He writes three lines to show any reeve of this coast: the boat is on Saint Felix's errand and is to be let alone. The steersman carries the leaf himself and will not let it near the bilge.
Give him the sack, and take his freight and a relic for the mast

He turns the gold in the light for a long time and sets it down gently. A thousand pennies of freight, paid ahead. The leaf that puts the boat on Saint Felix's errand. And a strip of linen that lay a night on Saint Botolph's tomb at Icanho, sewn in a leather bag, to hang at the mast. The Northman looks at the bag. Then he hangs it for you, since he ties the best knots aboard.
Give him the king's gear, and take his freight, a relic, and the cross in your name

It takes two clerks an afternoon to write down what is laid on the porch floor. Fifteen hundred pennies of freight, paid ahead. The leaf. The linen from Saint Botolph's tomb. And on the hoe an oak cross with a line cut in it by your lookout, who asked to do it: that a shipman of Dorestad gave this. The helm the bishop will not melt. He puts it in the chest with the relics and tells nobody why.

The porch of a small stone and timber church above a grey sea: an old bishop with ink on his thumb holding a small gold thing up to the light; the Frisian steersman kneeling; through the door, far along the shore, a new oak cross on a hill of mounds.
The finder's third
The reeve has the king's word, and two of the king's thegns to see it done. A board is set on the strand with a scale on it. Half the town has found a reason to be near.
My men opened the small hill by the fallen thorn on your word. It took them four days and they complained throughout. A cup, buckles, gold off a sword. It has gone to the king.
The sack is weighed and told over before witnesses. A cup, buckles, gold off a sword. It goes to the king.

I have been reeve here eleven winters and I never answered for a helm with a face before. Nor for a hole that size in the king's hill. But the word is that the finder is to be paid and not asked how. So.
The king's word is this. A third to the finder, by weight. And the boat to go free of toll at this strand for as long as she swims.
It is the first gold our young king has had that Offa did not weigh first. He was glad of it. He asked your name.
It goes to Offa, with the rest of what was ours. He will not ask your name. He will ask the weight.
It goes west to the Mercians. It will be rings on the arms of men who never saw the Deben.
At the back of the crowd an old woman with a fleece under her arm looks at the scale, and then at you, and goes home.
This year the reeve at Gipeswic sent the king gold out of the mounds on the Deben, and the finder had his share.
Take the finder's share and the king's leaf

Seven hundred pennies, counted on the board before everybody. And a leaf of parchment in Latin with the king's cross on it and four witnesses' crosses under: this boat pays no toll at Gipeswic. The reeve has a clerk read it aloud, because that is how it is done, and because he wants the town to hear who told.
Hand over the sack for the finder's share and the king's leaf

Eleven hundred pennies, weighed against the sack and counted on the board. And a leaf of parchment in Latin with the king's cross on it and four witnesses' crosses under: this boat pays no toll at Gipeswic. The reeve has a clerk read it aloud, because that is how it is done, and because he wants the town to hear who dug.
Hand over the king's gear for the finder's share, the leaf, and a seat among the king's merchants

Two thousand pennies. It takes the reeve and both thegns to count it, and they count it twice. The leaf with the king's cross: no toll at Gipeswic while the boat swims. And the thegns' word that the king will know your face in his hall and name you among the merchants who are his own. The helm is packed in straw. Nobody in the town has spoken to you since morning.

The strand at Gipeswic at noon: a trestle board with a scale and heaped pennies; a reeve and two thegns with gilded sword hilts; a clerk reading from a parchment leaf; a silent crowd, and at the back one old woman turning away.
After dark, by the back

After dark, by the back, without the Northman. The goldsmith has hung a hide over the door and lit one lamp. His wife counts what you lay on the bench. He does not look at it yet. He is looking at his crucible, which is already hot.
By Martinmas this will be a count's wife's brooches, a ring for an abbot, and the corner pieces of a book at Traiectum. Nobody will know it. That is what melting is for.
One of gold for twelve of silver, less my fire and my silence. My silence is dearer than my fire.
The top piece of the sword I would keep, if I were you. Not to sell. It is the only bit of this a man could hand his son and say what it was.
The helm I do not want to break. It is mostly iron, and it looks at me. Keep it or sink it. Or pay me to do what I would rather not.
Your steersman has gone to the church by the dam and has not come back. The Northman is on the boat with his sea chest packed. He has not said he is going. He has not said he is staying.
Sell it, and keep the sword's gold pommel

Thirteen hundred pennies in three bags, counted by his wife, who is quicker. The pommel he prises off whole and gives back in a twist of wool: gold, with the stepped red stones. By morning the rest is four small bars, and by evening he has sold two. The Northman is still aboard. He says he will stay to the season's end and then see.
Sell the gold and the silver, and keep the helm

Twenty-two hundred pennies. It takes until cockcrow and two crucibles. The Greek dishes go last: he reads the stamps on them with his lips and says a dead emperor's name. The helm goes back to the boat in a sack of bran. On the boat the Northman's place is empty, and his oar is laid along the thwart with the blade toward the land.
Sell it all, the helm too, and have him speak for you at the shipwright's

Twenty-five hundred pennies. The helm he breaks for its silver wire and its red stones, which takes an hour, and which he does with his mouth shut tight. His wife's brother is a wright on the slip below the dam: for a man with this much coin there is a keel's place next winter, and he will say so. On the boat the Northman's place is empty, and his oar is laid along the thwart with the blade toward the land.

A goldsmith's lean-to at night, one lamp and a white-hot crucible: on the bench a helm with a man's face looking straight out at the viewer, crushed silver dishes, a great gold buckle; the goldsmith's wife counting pennies into a bag.
